items.title: 16.7 Tests for identification of basic radicals

source_refs.note: Topic 16.7 with the copper-ammonia figure, printed pages 345-347, and Quick Check 16.4, printed at the top of page 348. The print labels both iron tests 'f)'.

blocks.text: Take 4 g of solid sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in about 10 cm³ distilled water. Divide this solution into two parts for further tests.

blocks.caption: Identification of aluminium radical
rows: To one part, add about 5 cm³ NaOH solution.
A white gelatinous precipitate is formed.
Al³⁺ ions are indicated.
To the second part of the above solution, add a few drops of aqueous ammonia.
A white precipitate is formed.
Al³⁺ ions are indicated

blocks.caption: Identification of ammonium radical
rows: Take 4 g of sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ distilled water. Add NaOH solution and gently heat it.
Ammonia gas is evolved with a distinct smell. Ammonia gas turns moist red litmus blue.
NH₄¹⁺ ions are indicated.

blocks.text: Take 4 g solid sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ distilled water. Make two parts of this solution for further tests.

blocks.caption: Identification of calcium radical
rows: To one part, add NaOH solution.
White precipitate is formed which does not dissolve in excess of NaOH solution.
Ca²⁺ ions are indicated.
To the second part of the above solution, add aqueous ammonia.
Only a slight turbidity appears or No precipitate is formed.
Ca²⁺ ions are indicated.

blocks.text: Add 4 g sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ distilled water. Make two parts of the above solution for further tests.

blocks.caption: Identification of chromium radical
rows: To one part, add NaOH solution.
A green precipitate appears which turns into green solution when excess of NaOH is added
Cr³⁺ ions are indicated.
To the second part of the above solution, add aqueous ammonia.
A green precipitate appears which is insoluble in excess of aqueous ammonia.
Cr³⁺ ions are indicated.

blocks.text: Add 4g solid sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10cm³ of distilled water. Make two parts of the above solution for further tests.

blocks.caption: Identification of copper radical
rows: To first part, add NaOH solution.
A light-blue precipitate is formed.
Cu²⁺ ions are indicated.
To the second part of the above solution, add aqueous ammonia.
Deep blue solution is formed.
Cu²⁺ ions are indicated.

blocks.alt: Three test tubes: pale blue [Cu(H2O)6]2+; with a small amount of ammonia a blue precipitate [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2] (ammonia acting as a base); with an excess of ammonia a deep blue solution [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (ligand exchange reaction).
blocks.caption: Copper(II) ions with a small amount and an excess of ammonia (original drawing after the figure printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: Take 4 g sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ of distilled water. Make two portions of the solution for further tests.

blocks.caption: Identification of iron (II) radical
rows: To one portion, add NaOH solution.
A green precipitate is formed which is turned into orange brown precipitate after some time.
Fe²⁺ ions are indicated.
To second portion of the above solution, add aqueous ammonia.
A white gelatinous precipitate of Fe(OH)₂ is formed which quickly oxidizes to form red brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃.
Fe²⁺ ions are indicated.

blocks.text: Take 2 g FeCl₃ in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ of distilled water. Make two portions of the solution for further tests.

blocks.caption: Identification of iron (III) radical
rows: To one portion, add NaOH solution.
Orange brown precipitate is formed.
Fe³⁺ ions are indicated.
To the second portion of the above solution, add aqueous ammonia.
Orange brown precipitate is formed.
Fe³⁺ ions are indicated.

blocks.text: Take 4 g solid sample in a clean test tube. Dissolve it in 10 cm³ of distilled water. Make two portions of the above solution for further tests.

blocks.caption: Identification of zinc radical
rows: To one portion add NaOH solution.
White precipitate is formed which is soluble in excess of NaOH solution.
Zn²⁺ ions are indicated.
To second portion of the above solution add aqueous ammonia.
White precipitate is formed which dissolves in excess of ammonia.
Zn²⁺ ions are indicated.
